newsitem.title: UK: UK government faces fresh row over meat safety.
newsitem.headline: UK government faces fresh row over meat safety.

text.p: The British government defended itself on Wednesday against allegations that it had ignored warnings about meat safety despite the crisis over mad cow disease and a food poisoning outbreak in Scotland which killed 20.

Opposition Labour member of parliament Nigel Griffiths said meat inspection officials in north east England wrote to Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg last year saying staff shortages meant they could not properly enforce rules designed to stop the spread of mad cow disease.
Hogg said he had not received the letter. But he rejected suggestions that controls to stop the spread of mad cow disease -- or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) -- were inadequate.

"I'm not aware of this letter. I'm very happy to accept that it was sent. I don't know why it was not responded to," said Hogg, who has been under fire for a week over his handling of the BSE crisis,which has led to an export ban on British beef.

"But on the substantive issue of the controls, they are rigorously and vigorously enforced within the abattoirs by the meat hygiene service whose numbers have been very substantially reinforced to make that possible," Hogg told the BBC.
Last week Labour accused the government of covering up a damning report on hygiene standards in British abattoirs.

Griffiths, Labour consumer affairs spokesman, said: "What the report tells Douglas Hogg is that a significant number of significant breaches of the legal requirement occurred including, they state, false claims that the meat was BSE-free.

Labour, widely expected to win the general election that must be called by May, has vowed to create a Food Standard Agency independent of the Agriculture Ministry to ensure consumer interests are not sacrificed to those of farmers.

Hogg accused Labour of making political capital out of the crisis in the meat industry. "We are in the last few weeks of this parliament, leading up to a general election. The Labour Party are trying to put whatever spin they can on these matters," he said.
Labour followed up last week's accusations by publishing on Tuesday a letter to junior agriculture minister Angela Browning from Peter Comrie, the Association of Meat Inspectors' general secretary.
Comrie said some inspectors had been threatened for trying to take action over breaches of hygiene in abattoirs and warned that falling standards were creating "a potential timebomb".

Hogg's defiant stand on Wednesday failed to dispel an image of muddle in the government's handling of the BSE crisis, which has cost the government 3.5 billion pounds ($5.62 billion) in compensation to farmers and other expenses.
But Major could not remove him this close to the election without damaging still further his dwindling chances of reeling in Labour's 20 point poll lead. ($1=.6228 Pound)
